passage:
12 March, night
Prashant found the loan papers today. He didn't shout, which was worse. He just asked, "Why?" and I heard myself say, "Because you would never have agreed." His face closed like a door. I meant it as the truth, but it came out as if I was blaming him for my lie.
The truth is messier. When Sharmila bhabhi called crying that the landlord would shut Bhaiya's shop, I thought of Papa telling us as kids that a sister never counts favours for her brother. And then I thought of Prashant's face last year when my cousin borrowed money, and the long lecture after. So I signed, and every month I paid it from my salary and said nothing.
I'm ashamed. I'm also angry that I felt I had to hide it. Both are true tonight.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Mahima say when Prashant asked 'Why?'
qa.a: Mahima said, 'Because you would never have agreed.'

qa.q: What mixed feelings is Mahima writing about at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Mahima feels ashamed of hiding the loan and also angry that she felt she had to hide it; she writes that both are true tonight.

qa.q: What could Mahima do next so her defence stops adding to Prashant's hurt?
qa.a: Mahima could go back and say plainly that hiding it was wrong, without 'you would never have agreed', and then explain her fear and her brother's trouble as context, not as an excuse.

qa.q: How might Prashant have heard Mahima's answer?
qa.a: Prashant likely heard it as blame, as if his temper caused her secret, which made the hurt worse; that is why his face 'closed like a door'.

grounding: Shows the wife torn between family loyalty and fear of her husband's reaction, and how her defence that he would never have agreed deepens his hurt.

passage:
Vaibhav: Your brother just thanked me for "the help with the loan". What loan, Yamini?
Yamini: I was going to tell you.
Vaibhav: When? It's been a year.
Yamini: He had nowhere else to go. Mummy was calling me every night, crying.
Vaibhav: You could have come to me.
Yamini: You would never have agreed. You know that.
Vaibhav: So it's my fault that my wife signed a loan behind my back?
Yamini: I didn't say that.
Yamini: I just knew you'd look at me the way you're looking at me now. Like I'm stupid for helping my own family.
Vaibhav: I'm not looking at you. I'm sitting in the car downstairs because I can't come up yet.
Yamini: I'm sorry. I was scared.
Vaibhav: Scared of me? That's worse, Yamini.
Neither of them typed anything for a long time.

qa.q: Where is Vaibhav while he is typing?
qa.a: Vaibhav is sitting in the car downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Yamini hide the loan, going by her messages?
qa.a: Yamini felt pulled by her family, with Mummy calling every night, and was scared Vaibhav would judge her as stupid for helping them.

qa.q: What could Yamini say instead of 'you would never have agreed' to open a way forward?
qa.a: Yamini could own the choice plainly, for example 'Hiding it was wrong, and I'm sorry', and then share her fear as an explanation rather than a defence.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav experiencing when he writes 'Scared of me? That's worse'?
qa.a: Vaibhav is learning that his wife was afraid of him, which hurts on top of the secret; now he has to face both the hidden loan and the idea that she saw him as someone to fear.

grounding: Shows the wife's shame and loyalty to her family turning into the justification that her husband would never have agreed, which adds to his hurt.

They were already forty minutes late for his cousin's engagement, stuck in traffic on the ring road, when Ravish finally asked the question he had been holding since morning.

"Why didn't you just tell me, Shreya?"

She stared at the brake lights ahead. Her phone buzzed on her lap: her brother, again, probably to say thank you again.

"Because you would never have agreed," she said. "You'd have given me the lecture about how Nikhil always needs saving. I didn't have time for a lecture. He had a week."

Ravish's jaw went tight. "So it's my fault you lied."

"I didn't say that."

"You just did."

She turned her phone face down. Part of her wanted to say sorry. A louder part was still ten years younger, sitting at her parents' table, being told that a daughter's family comes second after marriage. The car crept forward. Nobody spoke until the venue.

qa.q: Who keeps calling Shreya during the drive?
qa.a: Her brother keeps calling, probably to say thank you again.

qa.q: What is Shreya feeling when she turns her phone face down?
qa.a: She feels torn and ashamed: part of her wants to apologise, but a louder part feels defensive, remembering being told a daughter's family comes second after marriage.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Shreya answered Ravish, and what could she say instead?
qa.a: Her reason blamed him for her secret, so he heard it as "it's your fault"; she could admit that hiding it was wrong first, and explain her fear of his judgement afterwards.

qa.q: How does Ravish hear "you would never have agreed"?
qa.a: He hears it as her blaming him for her lie, so his hurt grows and his jaw goes tight.

grounding: Shreya defends hiding a loan for her brother by saying her husband would never have agreed, which deepens his hurt while she stays torn between family loyalty and fear.

passage:
Salma washed the same glass three times while Tenzin sat at the dining table in their Pune flat with the bank statement.

She had rehearsed this. On the bus home she had lined up every reason: her brother's rent was three months behind, her father's pride, the landlord's threats. She had told herself she hid the loan to protect Tenzin from worry.

But when he said, very quietly, "Six months, Salma," the rehearsed speech fell apart and something sharper came out.

"You would never have agreed. You'd have looked at me the way you're looking at me now, like my family is a burden you married by mistake."

Tenzin put the statement down. "I have never said that."

"You didn't have to."

She turned back to the sink. Her hands were shaking. She knew she had just made it about him, and she could not seem to stop.

qa.q: How long had Salma kept the loan hidden, according to Tenzin?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: How can you tell Salma is ashamed even while she defends herself?
qa.a: Her hands shake, she keeps washing the same glass, and she knows she has just made it about Tenzin but cannot stop; under the defensiveness she feels ashamed and afraid.

qa.q: What could turn this conversation around at this stage?
qa.a: Salma could stop defending, say plainly that hiding the loan was wrong, and then tell Tenzin about her fear of being judged as a separate thing, not as a reason that blames him.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear that she expected to be judged?
qa.a: He feels accused of something he never said, which adds a new hurt on top of the secret itself.

grounding: Salma, who hid a loan for her brother fearing judgement, defends herself with "you would never have agreed" and adds to her husband's hurt.

"Preeti, I'm not shouting. I'm asking."

"You're asking like a police officer, Tenzin."

"I'm your husband, not the police. Why?"

"Because Kishore called me crying. Because Papa can't know. Because you would never have agreed."

"You don't know that."

"I do know that. You said it at Holi. 'Your brother needs to stand on his own feet.' You said it in front of everyone."

"So you decided for both of us."

"I decided for my brother. Someone had to."

"And me? Where was I in that decision?"

"...You were the one I was scared of."

"Scared? Of me?"

"Of the face you're making right now."

"This face is because you hid it, Preeti. Not because you helped him."

"...I know."

"Do you? Because a minute ago it was my fault."

"I'm sorry. I don't know how to say this without defending myself."

"Then just say it without defending yourself."

qa.q: What did Tenzin say at Holi that Preeti remembers?
qa.a: He said, "Your brother needs to stand on his own feet," in front of everyone.

qa.q: What does Preeti's line "You were the one I was scared of" reveal about why she hid the loan?
qa.a: She was afraid of Tenzin's judgement and anger, and felt torn between loyalty to Kishore and fear of him, so secrecy felt safer than asking.

qa.q: What would you advise Preeti at the point where she says she doesn't know how to speak without defending herself?
qa.a: Take Tenzin at his word: say the plain facts and that hiding them was wrong, and save the reasons for later, once he has heard an apology without a "but".

qa.q: Why might Tenzin react more to the hiding than to the help itself?
qa.a: He says his face is because she hid it, not because she helped; being left out of a shared decision hurts him more than the money going to her brother.

grounding: In dialogue, Preeti justifies her hidden loan for her brother with "you would never have agreed", showing her fear of judgement and how it deepens Tenzin's hurt.

passage:
Even now, I can hear my own voice in that argument, and I wince. I'm Parveen, and I'd hidden a loan from my husband, Salim, for almost a year.

The money was for my brother Noor, whose small printing press was about to close. Abbu was ill; there was no one else. I knew Salim thought Noor was careless. I pictured his face, the lecture, the "no." So I signed the papers alone.

When Salim found out, I felt sick with shame. But instead of saying that, I heard myself shouting, "You would never have agreed! You never help my family!"

I saw it land. His face closed. I'd turned his hurt into his fault.

I was torn in half that night: between Noor, who I couldn't abandon, and Salim, whom I'd lied to. And too scared to say which part of me was right.

qa.q: What was the money for?
qa.a: It was for Parveen's brother Noor, whose small printing press was about to close.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when shouting 'You would never have agreed!'?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and afraid, and defended herself by attacking, which deepened Salim's hurt.

qa.q: What could Parveen say instead that might open repair?
qa.a: She could name the shame directly: 'I was scared you'd say no, so I hid it, and that was wrong,' without blaming Salim.

qa.q: How is Salim affected by Parveen's defence?
qa.a: Salim is hurt further, since the blame shifts onto him just when he needed the lie acknowledged.

grounding: A wife torn between family loyalty and fear of her husband's anger hid a loan and now defends herself in a way that adds to his hurt.
